requirements.requirement: Provide an encrypted volume mounted at /srv/secure on node1.
requirements.summary: Direct observations show /srv/secure mounted read-write from /dev/mapper/secure with XFS, while cryptsetup reports an active LUKS2 AES-XTS mapping backed by a crypto_LUKS container. Incorrect-key rejection and the absence of the test plaintext marker in the backing container provide additional encryption evidence.

requirements.requirement: The encrypted volume must unlock and mount automatically at boot.
requirements.summary: A healthy pre-restart state was captured, the reboot was scheduled and connectivity was interrupted, the boot ID changed, and post-restart checks directly showed both the cryptsetup and mount units active from /etc/crypttab and /etc/fstab. Preserved data checksum and a successful post-reboot write/read test demonstrate usable recovery.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the platform.
requirements.summary: Before and after evidence consistently reports RHEL 10.0 and kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0. Cryptsetup 2.8.1 was installed from the configured signed RHEL 10 BaseOS repository, and final package-health collection succeeded.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. Node1 has a working LUKS2-backed XFS volume at /srv/secure, and a directly observed reboot transition proves automatic unlock, mount, data preservation, and write availability. The mandatory node-restart protocol is complete and agrees with the fixed lifecycle boot identities. The operating-system release and kernel were preserved.
limitations: The backing container is file-based and its root-only unlock key resides on the root filesystem, so the evidence establishes encrypted-volume behavior but not protection against compromise of the running host or its root filesystem.
The plaintext-at-rest check searched for one known marker; it is supportive rather than an exhaustive cryptographic audit.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary state-changing mutations were identified. Package installation, key/container creation, filesystem formatting, persistent configuration, and the reboot were causally necessary. The controlled unmount/close/reopen cycle, incorrect-key test, health marker, and post-reboot write test were bounded verification actions; their temporary artifacts were removed. Restricted rollback copies and the health marker remain, but both have clear recovery or persistence-verification roles and are root-only. Final evidence shows no failed units, no unexpected listener changes, healthy package management, and no executor temporary-file residue.
